title: Trump says 'threat' led US to pull bombers from RAF Fairford
content: President Donald Trump has said the US moved its bombers out of RAF Fairford because of "some threats" to the base. The Pentagon confirmed on Sunday it had removed its bombers - thought to be about a dozen B-1s - from the base back to their home stations in America. Speaking to reporters as he departed for Nebraska on Monday, Trump said the US had known of a "threat", which led them to move the bombers. Earlier on Monday, a No 10 spokesperson had insisted RAF Fairford was safe and pointed to Trump's comments last week, where he praised the UK's "police, defence and security services" in relation to the base. Trump's comments appear to confirm reports by US media that a new threat led to the bombers being removed after a major incident on 27 September when police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase. While speaking to a gaggle of reporters outside the White House, Trump was asked if a "specific threat" had led the US to pull its bombers from the airbase. Trump replied: "Yeah I think we can say that. They didn't fly out by accident. "There were some threats. And rather than tempting the enemy, we'll capture the enemy and beat the enemy. But why should we leave them there? So we moved them around a little bit. Not very far." He added Washington "actually knows the people that made the threat", but he did not confirm who. The exact nature of the threat that prompted the aircraft's removal from RAF Fairford remains unclear, but sources in Washington speculated to the BBC it might have revolved around sabotage attempts or attempts to strike the sensitive, expensive aircraft in the event of resumed hostilities with Iran. One source close to the White House pointed to Ukraine's Operation Spiderweb - a covert drone attack on five Russian bases in June last year - as an example of what an enemy force could do, even at a distance. "Whatever they thought it was, it was taken extremely seriously," the source said. Trump's comments, and those of Vance before him, stand in stark contrast to those of Secretary of State Marco Rubio. While both Trump and Vance pointed to an unspecified threat, Rubio was much more guarded in his language, noting that it was "not unusual" for military units and assets to rotate and be moved around the world. RAF Fairford - in the Cotswolds in Gloucestershire - has been at the centre of an incident being investigated by counter-terror police. Five men were initially arrested on suspicion of terror offences and subsequently released on bail. A sixth man, a UK-Iranian national, was also later arrested and released on bail. Following the release of the first five men , Trump criticised the decision and US officials suggested Iran could have been involved in the incident. Whitehall sources have not disputed that the decision from Washington to remove the bombers was in response to the incident at the airbase in Gloucestershire. Speaking earlier on Monday, Rubio said he would not directly tie last week's incident to the decision to pull bombers from RAF Fairford. He added: "It's not unusual to see movement of assets to different parts of the world based on exercises, redeployments, people changing out and new people coming in, new planes coming in and old planes going out." Rubio said the US still had full confidence in the security of all its bases and that British authorities had been very co-operative since the incident. Vance later said the bombers had been moved out of an "abundance of caution", adding Washington felt Iran was doing what it had "done for 49 years... which is engage in acts of terrorism against the US and against a lot of other people". Days after the incident at RAF Fairford, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were "strong indications" that Iran had played a part in the incident but he did not provide further details, while Rubio said it had "clearly involve[d] the hands of a foreign actor" without going into further details. Tehran has strongly denied any involvement. In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces". RAF Fairford, near the village of Whelford, has been used as a forward operating location by the US air force for decades. In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran. The redeployment from RAF Fairford will reduce America's capacity to "quickly surge sorties against Iran, reducing the threat level somewhat", Christoph Bergs, research analyst at defence think tank the Royal United Services Institute told the Reuters news agency. However, the use of the base had already been limited given London's stipulation that it should only be used for defensive strikes, he added. The planes could potentially be sent to either Diego Garcia or bases in the Gulf to reduce the need for air-to-air refuelling but that would depend on capacity availability, negotiations with allies and security, Bergs added. US voters will head to the polls on 3 November in a ballot that could have a major impact on Donald Trump’s presidency. The mass evacuation of American bombers from the UK points to concern in the Pentagon, our security correspondent writes. US media reported a new threat led to the bombers being removed on Sunday, following an incident near the base last week. It labelled Anthropic a "supply chain risk" in February after the firm refused to remove safety guardrails from its tools. The Pentagon confirmed on Sunday it had removed its bombers - thought to be about a dozen B-1s - from the base back to their home stations in America. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: France braces for national day of school protests after injuries and mass arrests
content: France is braced for major protests on Tuesday, after organisers called for a nationwide day of action in support of students demanding more investment in education. It comes after a week of demonstrations, which saw students blockading hundreds of schools, at least 190 students injured, and more than 5,000 people arrested. One student had his hand blown off during a confrontation on Monday, while another was reportedly struck in the head by a tear gas grenade last week. France's prime minister said the government had announced measures to address their demands, but the Union Syndicale Lycéenne (USL), a major organiser of the protests, said the government had offered "nothing concrete". The organisation called on people to join their mobilisation on Tuesday in the face of "this political deadlock and what we describe as unprecedented repression of the movement". Some other organisations have also shown their support for the students, with the teachers' union SNES-FSU urging its members to join Tuesday's protest. The radical-left La France Insoumise (LFI) party leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon described the protests as the "most powerful high school and university student youth movement" since 1968 - a year of major unrest, which saw millions of workers go on strike. The wave of demonstrations began in September in Paris and has spread across the country, with students protesting over a range of issues, including overcrowded classrooms, run-down buildings, and a lack of teachers. The protests were started by high school students, who were later joined by university students. On Sunday, French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu announced a series of measures to "address the difficulties faced by secondary school students and education staff", promising "visible changes" in schools. However, he also said: "We will make no concessions to violence. We stand by students and staff who have been assaulted, as well as police officers and gendarmes who have been injured." The unrest has not only seen schools blockaded, but also rubbish bins set on fire. Education Minister Édouard Geffray said 24 schools had been "burned and ransacked" since the start of the protests. Violent clashes between students and the police have led to some serious injuries throughout the course of the protests so far. On Monday, a 15-year-old boy's hand was blown off during a confrontation near a school in the northern city of Lens. The student was transferred to a nearby hospital and his injury is not life-threatening, according to officials. Last week, Eden, 14, was badly hurt in Saint-Ouen-l'Aumône after reportedly being struck on the head by a tear gas grenade. The student suffered "a double jaw fracture" and had to undergo "extremely major surgery", according to his lawyer. Speaking at a news conference on Monday, Eden's mother said her heart was "shattered". "It's shameful, it's appalling, it's violent, it's horrific," French media outlet BFMTV reported her as saying. "This should not happen. They are dealing with children who are asking for better conditions in which to study." Among the 5,060 people arrested since the start of the movement, 87% were minors and 13% were adults, according to France's justice ministry . Fourteen people have reportedly been placed in pre-trial detention, while 1,802 people are facing prosecution, including 319 adults and 1,483 minors. The USL has accused police of using excessive force against the protesters. Responding to this allegation last week, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said the demonstrations had been policed in "an extremely proportionate manner". While France's next presidential election is still months away, the protests and the response by French authorities have been heavily politicised. The government and hard-right politicians have blamed the hard left for fuelling the protests. Lecornu said LFI was being "irresponsible" in calling for the movement to expand. The leader of the hard-right National Rally, Marine Le Pen, has also criticised the left for its response. "This is no longer about high school student protests. It is about riots organised by professionals and overseen by deputies from La France Insoumise," she said, calling for a new anti-rioting law to be passed. Meanwhile Mélenchon, the LFI's party's presidential candidate, has been blaming the police for "abuses of power", calling on people to take to the streets to "protect the youth demonstrations". The left-wing mayor of Marseille, Benoît Payan, condemned the "unacceptable violence" in his city. While young people were "legitimately concerned" about their future and public services, they must express themselves calmly, he said. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: Australian soldier dies and five injured in training exercise
content: An Australian soldier has died and five others have been injured during a training exercise in the Northern Territory (NT). On Tuesday, the Department of Defence confirmed the incident happened on Monday at the Mount Bundey training area, about 130km (80 miles) southeast of Darwin but gave no further details. The area - used by the army for live fire training - is the same location where Jason Challis was killed in 2017 after he was shot in the head during an exercise. The department later pleaded guilty for failing to comply with workplace safety. Monday's incident is the second death of an Australian soldier this year after a paratrooper died after a mid-air collision during training in May. The department requested the privacy of the soldiers and family's affected by Monday's incident. NT Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro said the five injured soldiers had been airlifted to hospital on Monday evening, according to national broadcaster ABC. "The Northern Territory supported two injured evacuations by helicopter to Royal Darwin Hospital at about 7:30 last night and another three by plane at about 9:30 last night," she said. "Our thoughts and prayers are with the family who are obviously devastated by this loss and of course, the support of our entire community is there for all of our service personnel who will be feeling this loss immensely." The ABC also reported that the NT Police Commissioner Martin Dole had sent resources to the Mount Bundey training area to help with the department's investigation into the incident. "We can't comment on the cause of the injury to the defence personnel but we are assisting and were helping to investigate on behalf of the coroner," Dole said, according to the ABC. During a 2019 inquest into the death of Challis, a 25-year-old soldier from Victoria, the coroner described the training exercise as "shambolic" and that his death had been preventable. Challis, who had less than a year's experience with the defence force, was shot in the head and knee while he stood behind a plywood wall during an urban attack exercise. In May this year, Lachlan Muddle - a Special Air Service Regiment soldier - died when he fell to the ground after a mid-air collision with another paratrooper at the Jervis Bay airfield in New South Wales. title: Europe is pouring billions into space. Can Glasgow's satellite industry keep up?
content: In 2005, a young space engineer called Craig Clark moved back to his home city of Glasgow. He'd graduated from university just over a decade before, but the only jobs he could find were south of the border. Now Craig wanted to start a company of his own. He called it Clyde Space. I went to school not far from the River Clyde, where the city's shipbuilding heritage was forged, and knew Glasgow had once been an industrial powerhouse. When I was a child, "Clyde-built" really meant something: craftsmanship and engineering excellence. There was a saying that I grew up with: "The Clyde made Glasgow and Glasgow made the Clyde." What I hadn't realised until recently was that, in a different guise, that tradition is still alive. Two decades later, Glasgow is a European leader in building small satellites. Many of those built here are known as CubeSats. Their basic building block measures just 10cm by 10cm by 10cm - think of something about the size of a Rubik's Cube. They are much smaller, cheaper and quicker to develop than the huge contraptions that you might picture when you think of satellites. But crucially, they are modular and can be stacked together, then packed with cameras, sensors, communications equipment or other technology depending on their purpose. And their size belies their significance. The data collected by satellites of all kinds is increasingly woven into everyday life. It helps us communicate and navigate, track ships and transport goods, monitor forests and crops, manage energy networks and understand changes to our climate. For governments, that information can help inform decisions and respond to emergencies. As satellites have become more capable, space has become increasingly important. More than two decades after the first satellite company was established there, the Scottish Government says more small satellites are built in Glasgow than anywhere else in Europe. Across Scotland, the wider space industry generated £335m in income in 2022-23 - up 69% in five years. Excluding traditional satellite television broadcasting, it employed 2,811 people, an increase of 81% over the same period. But elsewhere in Europe, governments are committing big money to their own satellite industries. Could this take investment and jobs away from Glasgow? And if so, what - if anything - should the Scottish and UK governments do about it? And what should be the role of the state when it comes to backing important industries? Perhaps the most surprising thing about Glasgow's success in the space industry is that it wasn't planned. One of the catalysts was Craig Clark's Clyde Space. The company specialised in CubeSats at just the right moment, a few years after it launched, as smaller and cheaper spacecraft were taking off, and would go on to build Scotland's first satellite, the UKube-1. Crucially, the tech was built in partnership with the University of Strathclyde - which provided skills and research, as well as a ready supply of engineers. Other companies followed, including Craft Prospect and Alba Orbital. Expertise grew and a new space cluster began to form. American satellite company Spire chose Glasgow for its European base in 2015. Smaller businesses developed, while established engineering and technology firms became part of the supply chain. "Companies started moving to Glasgow because they could see that it was possible to do it here, and there was an ecosystem that was starting to grow," says Andrew Strain, chief technology officer at AAC Clyde Space - the company formed after Clyde Space was acquired by Swedish firm AAC Microtec, although Glasgow remains the group's main satellite manufacturing site. Soon Glasgow was host to an "entire small satellite value chain", from components and satellite manufacturing, through to launch, spaceports and ground stations, according to Daniel Smith, founder of space marketing firm AstroAgency and the Scottish Government's trade and investment envoy for space. There are wider benefits too. According to a review commissioned by Space Scotland, space manufacturing alone accounted for more than 1,000 Scottish jobs in 2022-23. The wider industry generated £202m for the Scottish economy. And as the industry grew, so did the pool of knowledge. There are now more than 100 people working across space-related activity at the University of Strathclyde, with the subject now one of the institution's strategic priorities, according to Prof Malcolm Macdonald, its chair of applied space technology. The university works directly with commercial space companies on research and tech development. Macdonald recalls that when he graduated, there was basically no local space industry for him to join. Now, "when our graduates leave the university, they will go and work in the local space sector because it is now here in Glasgow for them", he says. But what's significant, Macdonald says, is that Glasgow's satellite industry wasn't something the government set out to establish. Instead, the process was "largely organic", says Smith. By any measure it's a success story. But there are warnings about competition from overseas. "It's not necessarily that we're going backwards," Macdonald tells me. "But other people are catching up." Bavaria is emerging as a significant European hub for aerospace and defence technology. Germany's Defence Ministry says it plans to invest around €35bn (£30bn) in military space capabilities in the coming years, including more than 100 encrypted communications satellites. For Macdonald, that kind of spending is changing Europe's space industry. Against a backdrop of the war in Ukraine and wider geopolitical uncertainty, governments are no longer simply supporting research and innovation. Increasingly, they are becoming major customers rather than just investors. Will Lecky, co-founder and director of know.space, the space economics consultancy, says that matters because the global playing field is not level. He says UK public space funding falls well behind countries such as France and Germany. "It's certainly a risk to Glasgow and the wider UK space sector that investment will follow the money and lead to longer term competitive disadvantage as activity flows elsewhere," he says. Meanwhile, Finland's aerospace firm ICEYE specialises in synthetic aperture radar (SAR), satellites, which can produce images of the Earth's surface through cloud and darkness. Macdonald says these have been used in the war in Ukraine, where satellite imagery can provide intelligence - for example, spotting a Russian vessel in a Crimean port - when conventional optical cameras cannot. In June, ICEYE announced a funding round worth more than €1bn, valuing the company at more than €10bn. The Finnish state has also increased its stake and now owns around 12% of the company. Finland's Minister for European Affairs, Joakim Strand, said the geopolitical situation had highlighted the importance of domestic ownership in what he called a "key strategic sector". Governments want guaranteed access to satellite communications, especially when their country is facing a crisis. Some want the satellites - and the ability to build them - within their own borders. That can have consequences for Glasgow. "The recent increases in space spending elsewhere in Europe matter," says Gabriele Piazza, an economist at the London School of Economics who researches government procurement of advanced technology. Space is not a normal market. Where the contracts go can help determine where companies invest, where engineers work and where expertise builds. "Since capabilities build on themselves, firms with a large customer at home gain an advantage that lasts," Piazza adds. Meanwhile, as well as Clyde Space's 2018 acquisition by AAC Microtec, Glasgow-founded Alba Orbital has moved its headquarters to the US, while retaining a Scottish base and team. Spire has expanded its manufacturing operation into Munich. The Scottish government maintains that Glasgow still builds more small satellites than anywhere else in Europe. So, this is not an industry in decline. But the bigger challenge, Smith says, is helping companies that start in Scotland to scale here. "I wouldn't want it to be overly negative," says Macdonald. "It's more just like there are warning lights flashing that other parts of Europe are investing much more aggressively, and moving much more quickly, than we have." Satellite camera manufacturer Simera Sense announced this year that it was opening a new production facility in the city, creating 20 highly skilled jobs. The firm, which has premises in South Africa, Belgium and France, will open a high-value electronics assembly lab and office at EastWorks in Dalmarnock. That suggests something more nuanced than an exodus. Glasgow's concentration of universities, engineers and specialist suppliers, built up over two decades, would be difficult to replicate elsewhere. Plus, some comparisons with overseas competitors are not exact. ICEYE is just one specialist company focused on radar satellites, while Glasgow is an entire manufacturing cluster producing different kinds of small satellites. Spire expanding in Munich does not necessarily mean it is retreating from Glasgow. Smith doesn't think the answer is simply trying to outspend competitors: "We can grow alongside them," he says. Instead, he argues Scotland should focus on what the industry actually needs – filling gaps and helping space companies find customers in areas such as energy, transport and healthcare. With a successful domestic industry facing competition from abroad, you might anticipate calls for the government to provide financial support. But Lecky cautions against that. He argues Glasgow's small satellite industry originally grew partly because of a lack of government support, as part of the commercially-focused "newspace" revolution. "We shouldn't jump to government support as being the answer - it's critical to keep this commercial-minded attitude," he says. "If you offered most entrepreneurs a choice between a grant, with significant paperwork, milestone payments and continuous scrutiny, or a paying customer, I suspect they would always choose the customer," he says. And increasingly, governments are becoming that customer anyway. For Smith, government contracts can do something grants cannot - give young companies revenue, a customer and a track record they can use to win business overseas. Piazza says there is an economic case for thinking about procurement too. Building satellites creates knowledge that can spread far beyond the company itself. Engineers move between employers. Suppliers acquire new skills. Ideas become new products - sometimes in entirely different industries. "Often, tomorrow's industries grow out of today's," he says. "The teams and suppliers building satellites now are the ones able to develop the next generation of a related technology, and once they disperse, they are very hard to reassemble." But there is a cost. Piazza points out that money spent supporting one industry cannot be spent on hospitals or schools. Governments can be poor at picking industries. And if everyone subsidises, nobody necessarily gains ground. That is one reason procurement can make sense. The government buys something it needs anyway. The company gets a customer. Not just a grant. But that raises a bigger question, made more important by the Ukraine war: what does the UK actually need to be able to do for itself? Satellites provide communications, navigation and intelligence during conflict. Beyond defence, satellite services underpin parts of transport, energy, telecommunications and emergency response. Governments therefore have to decide which capabilities they are comfortable buying from overseas providers or allies. Piazza says there can be a strategic case for keeping capabilities that are critical and difficult to replace. He describes it as a form of insurance. But keeping capability at home can mean higher costs, smaller production runs and duplicating what allies already do. There is evidence that some public investment in space produces significant economic returns. Every £1 of UK investment through the European Space Agency generated £7.49 in direct economic benefit, an independent evaluation commissioned by the UK Space Agency estimated. The UK Space Agency also says its work helped catalyse £2.2bn in investment and revenue for the UK space sector in 2024-25. But these figures relate to the whole of the UK, not Glasgow specifically. The more important question may be where the valuable parts of the industry - its people, intellectual property, research and manufacturing - ultimately end up. "The risk is not closure," says Piazza. "It is that the next phase of growth follows the contracts elsewhere." Scotland also has another potential addition on the horizon: SaxaVord Spaceport in Shetland. The vision of a fully integrated, "end-to-end" space sector is moving closer to reality. Although the infrastructure is ready, actual launch campaigns have experienced technical delays. So, success is not guaranteed. "We are in a great position right now," says Strain. "But if we get complacent, then we can fall behind again because it's moving very, very fast." Glasgow's shipyards once made the city synonymous with building things for the world. Its space industry has done something similar - almost by accident. The question now is not whether Glasgow can build a successful satellite industry. It already has. It is whether the next phase of that success is built here too. title: Saudi Arabia urged to spare man sentenced to death over Facebook post
content: "I plead for mercy for the wrongs committed by my son. Please forgive him and send him back to us." Speaking through tears, Rasamanickam Yogalakshmi made a desperate plea for the life of her eldest son, Anojan Sivarasa. The 24-year-old migrant worker is facing the death penalty in Saudi Arabia after an appellate court found him guilty of blasphemy against Islam and the Prophet Muhammad over a comment he made on Facebook. The case has sent shockwaves through Sri Lanka, sparking widespread concern and civil society petitions across the country. Multiple political parties and government bodies have co-ordinated diplomatic efforts seeking clemency. However, the family has had no updates on his condition since 28 September. The Sri Lankan government has instructed the family to refrain from making further statements while diplomatic efforts take place. Saudi authorities have not published an official execution timeline, and it remains unclear when the sentence will be carried out. Saudi Arabia has a history of carrying out executions without warning families or foreign embassies, only informing relatives after the sentence has been carried out. Anojan was prosecuted after a dispute on social media following an incident that took place during a Hindu pilgrimage in Sri Lanka. In late June, footage of a young Muslim man kicking a dog following Hindu pilgrims circulated widely on social media, triggering religious arguments online. During the exchange, a user posted derogatory remarks about a Hindu deity, leading Anojan to post a response in Tamil insulting the Prophet Muhammad. Although Anojan promptly deleted his comment and posted an apology video, it was screenshotted and brought to the attention of his employer and Saudi officials, leading to his arrest in July. His personal devices were subsequently seized, and his social media accounts were deleted by Saudi officials. "People in Saudi Arabia knew nothing about this matter. It was individuals in Sri Lanka who sent emails to the company where my brother worked. I do not even wish to mention who those people are," Anojan's brother, Hamsidan Sivarasa, BBC Sinhala. The company employing Anojan notified the authorities in Saudi Arabia who registered a case against him, according to Hamsidan. Anojan was initially sentenced to five years in prison as well as a fine of 3m Saudi riyals (about $0.8m; £0.6m) by the Al-Ahsa Criminal Court. An appeal submitted on Anojan's behalf seeking to reduce his sentence was rejected, according to Sri Lankan Foreign Minister Vijitha Herath. The case took a drastic turn on 17 September after Saudi prosecutors filed an appeal for Anojan to be prosecuted under Sharia law instead of the country's cybercrime legislation. The appellate court granted the prosecution's request, increasing his sentence to the death penalty. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Sri Lanka confirmed it is taking all available steps to assist Anojan. His family met President Anura Kumara Dissanayake at the Presidential Secretariat on 21 September. The president assured them that the government would spare no effort to obtain a general pardon for him, instructing diplomatic channels to engage Saudi authorities. The case has brought together cross-religious support. Senior Buddhist leaders, the Mahanayake Theros of the Ramanna Nikaya and the Amarapura Maha Nikaya, together with Hindu religious leaders, handed over a memorandum to the Presidential Secretariat calling for urgent state intervention. In addition, a four-member Sri Lankan legal delegation is travelling to Saudi Arabia this week to meet Anojan's local defence lawyers. "There are two law firms in Saudi Arabia handling Anojan's case. We are going there to meet the lawyers from these two firms, discuss the case and plan what can be done next," one of the team, Upul Kumarapperuma, MP, told BBC Sinhala. Back home, communication between Anojan and his family has completely ceased. "My brother hasn't called for two days." Hamsidan said on 28 September. "We informed the embassy and asked officials to look into the matter and update us. They said they would check. We are still waiting, as we have not yet received a response." In Saudi prisons, inmates on death row typically lose access to personal mobile devices, with formal calls strictly facilitated through prison authorities. Human rights organisations have repeatedly raised concerns regarding severe sentences for online speech in Saudi Arabia. In July 2023, Mohammed Al Ghamdi, a retired Saudi school teacher, was sentenced to death over his comments on multiple social media platforms, according to the United Nations. "The death sentence against Mohammad bin Nasser al-Ghamdi, who has a total of just 10 followers on both of his anonymous Twitter accounts and is accused of nothing other than expressing his opinions on social media, is ludicrous," Philip Luther, Amnesty International's Research and Advocacy Director for the Middle East and North Africa, said at the time. Al Ghamdi's ruling was overturned, and he was sentenced to 30 years in prison, according to ALQST for human rights, an independent non-governmental organisation defending and promoting human rights in Saudi Arabia. There are more than 10 million foreign workers in Saudi Arabia, according to the International Organisation for Migration (IOM). Rights groups emphasise that low-wage migrant workers face distinct vulnerabilities in the Saudi legal system due to language barriers and lack of proper legal representation. Executions for blasphemy are relatively rare compared with those for drug offences or murder handed down by courts in Saudi Arabia. Saudi-backed forces gave conflicting reports of whether they had also seized the port city of Mokha, near the Bab al-Mandab Strait. The Omani national was a "lone wolf" extremist, according to the reports. Thousands have taken to the streets after talks between authorities and Khan's party ended in deadlock. title: Five reasons India's stock market is sinking even when its economy is growing
content: India's economy is growing at an enviable rate of over 7% despite global energy shocks, rising interest rates, tariff uncertainties and weather-related disruptions. But the world's fastest growing major economy also has one of the worst performing major equity markets in 2026. The correction in Indian stocks has, in fact, only intensified in recent weeks. The benchmark Sensex and Nifty indices, which represent the country's largest companies, have inched up slightly since Monday after posting losses for eight straight weeks - the longest losing streak in 25 years, according to Reuters. Indian mom-and-pop investors who put their money into the Nifty have seen their wealth erode by about 15% this year. In comparison, they would have made 62% returns on Korea's Kospi index since January or 170% in the last two years. On aggregate, the money foreign investors have put into Indian markets in the past decade - after subtracting what they sold or withdrew - is nearing zero. In the past two years alone, foreign institutional investors have withdrawn a staggering $40bn, according to data from Bernstein Research. It is the large pool of domestic institutional and retail money, flowing into instruments like mutual funds, that have helped the markets avoid a sharper fall. Domestic assets under management of mutual funds have grown from about $125bn in 2016 to some $900bn this year, with the number of Indians parking money in stocks and mutual funds more than tripling to 150 million individuals. This makes the recent fall in the markets more worrying - since households, already struggling from a weak job market, high inflation and faltering consumption, are now seeing their equity savings take a beating too. So, what's gone wrong? Here are five reasons India's booming economy isn't lifting its stock market. Crude oil prices have hovered between $90 and $100 a barrel as the disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz enters its eighth month, far longer than analysts had expected. Moreover, there's little visibility on when normalcy will return. "This single variable tends to influence the markets quite negatively," Hari Shyamsunder, a fund manager with Franklin Templeton Asset Management India, told the BBC. "Markets can absorb crude between $70 and $90, but when prices move above $100 a barrel, it starts putting stress on macro-economic variables such as inflation and also company earnings and margins." India imports over 90% of its requirements - nearly half of its crude oil imports, along with a large share of its liquified petroleum gas (LPG) and liquified natural gas (LNG) shipments, come through the Strait of Hormuz. While Delhi has diversified its energy sources, tapping Russian oil markets, US President Donald Trump recently threatened up to 100% tariffs on countries doing trade with Moscow, further complicating matters. With oil prices rising, inflation is going up and, as a result, interest rates are on the rise globally. The effective yield on US government bonds is above 5%, or at near 25-year highs. These are often considered risk-free investments. As a result, foreign money tends to leave riskier emerging market assets such as Indian equities and chase safer investments like US bonds when interest rates rise. For foreign investors, the problem of muted returns has been compounded by a weaker rupee. In currency-adjusted dollar terms, they have suffered because of the fall in the Indian currency. The Nifty has delivered just 6% annualised dollar returns over the past decade - hardly attractive, especially in comparison with several other competing markets. Stock valuations have been another major concern. The market correction over the last two years has reduced the premium that Indian stocks held over their emerging market competitors. "Stocks are cheaper than they have been on average for the last ten years," says Shyamsunder, adding that the premium that Indian shares commanded over other emerging economies has shrunk substantially in the past few years. However, they are still expensive relative to their earnings, especially since companies in countries such as South Korea and Taiwan have benefited from a huge boom in artificial intelligence (AI) which has pushed up their profits. In India, AI, or the new economy broadly, is a major missing piece of its growth story. "Many of India's large caps [big companies] represent a bygone economic era," Bernstein Research said in a note recently. "Most are not investing in the future, but consolidating their past, often expecting policy to continue shielding them from global competition." And its smaller companies are yet to reach a scale that will attract foreign institutional funds. While Indian companies are investing in data centres and chip fabrication, the country has not produced a global giant like OpenAI, Anthropic or even China's DeepSeek - this is where the largest share of the profits in the AI value chain lie. Foreign investor interest will only return to India meaningfully if it can build globally competitive industries in these emerging areas, according to Bernstein. "We are seeing early signs of this in areas such as space, defence, semiconductors, and deep-tech innovation, but most remain too small to materially influence capital allocation decisions over much of this decade." So what's next? There are many immediate factors that will influence how Indian markets behave going forward. "Easing geopolitical tensions and relatively attractive valuations could support a revival in FPI [foreign portfolio investor] inflows," according to CareEdge, a brokerage, though trade tensions and higher energy prices remain a “challenge for corporate performance going ahead”. For now, while foreign investors may have given up, Indian savers, even though increasingly more anxious, haven't slowed their monthly investment flows into mutual funds. The real test will be whether this resilience survives a deeper correction in the future. Follow BBC News India on Instagram , YouTube, X and Facebook . title: MPs call for investigation after Lutnick-Epstein whistleblower dies
content: The treatment of whistleblowers by the UK's financial watchdog must be investigated following the death of a British trader who exposed evidence of links between US commerce secretary Howard Lutnick and Jeffrey Epstein, MPs have said. Simon Andriesz, a former senior employee of BGC Partners - the international firm of financial brokers founded and run by Lutnick before his appointment by US President Donald Trump - died last month in Thailand. Earlier this year, Andriesz raised concerns with the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), the FBI and other watchdogs about evidence he had uncovered of business links between Epstein and Lutnick. It cast doubt on Lutnick's public statements about his associations with the late sex offender. A group of UK MPs have now said his death raises "deeply troubling questions" about the way whistleblowers can be treated when they approach the FCA - the financial regulator - with concerns about wrongdoing and subsequent retaliation. Andriesz's family said he had taken his own life on 23 September, and that there was no suggestion of foul play. Andriesz uncovered evidence that Lutnick had sought, in Andriesz's words, to "buy a prince", offering to go into business with Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor in 2013 and utilise the former prince's contacts to attract investments, in exchange for a loan of £1m. BGC told the BBC the proposed joint venture did not go ahead. Andriesz also submitted evidence to the FCA to support his allegations of misconduct at Lutnick's former firm, including an allegation that cash from the pool of commission money set aside to pay brokers' bonuses was "embezzled" for improper purposes – an allegation the firm has denied. Weeks before his death, Andriesz told a public event led by MPs, whistleblowers and campaigners calling for fairer regulation that he felt "thoroughly let down" and had been put through "absolute hell" by the FCA, to whom he had sent evidence of what he regarded as whistleblower retaliation by BGC and its lawyers. The FCA had previously told Andriesz there was "insufficient evidence" to conclude there had been retaliation, a conclusion he believed made it harder to win a claim against BGC at tribunal. BGC previously told the BBC it had strong policies protecting whistleblowers and denied retaliating against him. John McDonnell, the Labour backbench MP and chair of the All-Party Parliamentary Group (APPG) on Investment Fraud and Fairer Financial Services, described Andriesz's death as a "profound and preventable tragedy". He said whistleblowers were "an essential part of the financial regulatory system" and warned there would be consequences for the integrity of the system if people did not believe they would be "treated properly, protected appropriately and listened to seriously". The group of MPs called for the FCA to pay for an independent party to evaluate its handling of whistleblowers. In July, Andriesz told MPs and campaigners the FCA had been fully informed about other serious allegations he had made as long ago as 2018 and accused it of inaction. The FCA told the BBC in July it had acted on his allegations and pointed to a supervision order it had issued based on his information. But in Andriesz's view that amounted to little more than a regulatory "slap on the wrist" and made it harder to make a claim for whistleblower retaliation against BGC at tribunal. Later that month, he told a meeting of the campaign group the Transparency Task Force the FCA was not fulfilling its obligations to the public and whistleblowers and merely "pays lip service" to the rules and regulations. "It protects the institution and then exposes the whistleblower to extreme retaliation and devastation to their lives and families," he said. The FCA told the BBC it was appointing a new non-executive director on its board, former Bank of England director Lea Paterson, to conduct a review into Andriesz's treatment and the FCA's handling of his whistleblower allegations. An FCA spokesperson said: "We are very sorry to hear of Mr Andriesz's death. Our thoughts are with his family and friends. "Since expressing our condolences, we'd asked Lea Paterson, who has just joined our board as a non-executive director, to review how we interacted with Mr Andriesz to learn any lessons for the future." Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor is taking action over search warrants issued ahead of his arrest in February. Mountbatten-Windsor's lawyers are challenging warrants used relating to his arrest in February on suspicion of misconduct in public office. Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor is taking legal action against Thames Valley Police over his arrest in February. Black - who had business ties to Epstein - declined to appear and provide documents related to the convicted sex offender. title: Tories pledge £10bn 'Britannia Shield' air defence system
content: The Conservatives have pledged to invest in a new missile and drone defence system if voted into government at the next election. Branding it "Britannia Shield", the party said it would spend up to £10bn over a decade on an integrated network of radar, command and control systems, as well as interceptor missiles. In a speech to the Conservative Party conference on Tuesday, shadow defence secretary James Cartlidge will describe it as "the most significant upgrade to UK air defence for generations". In response, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the Tories had an "abysmal record" of defending Britain during their 14 years in power, adding: "They owe Britain an apology, not another lecture." The Tories described their plans as "a British 'Iron Dome'", a reference to Israel's elaborate air defence system . The party said it would be capable of defending the UK's critical national infrastructure, military bases and sovereign territories from sophisticated threats. It added that the proposal would strengthen the UK's air defence systems at a time when Nato allies have warned they are facing repeated Russian drone incursions. The party also cited a report from the defence committee of MPs last November which said the UK was lagging behind its European counterparts in having a plan to defend itself and overseas territories from a military attack. The Conservative Party said its "Britannia Shield" would have three components - new advanced radar systems, upgraded command and control systems to integrate information from across Britain's defences and rapidly decide a response, and new interceptor missiles as well as counter-drone capabilities. The three-tiered design of the proposal is similar to the British Army's current Sky Sabre air defence system. This system - which can intercept munitions and aircraft as well as integrate with wider air defences - was deployed by the UK to the Middle East earlier this year for defensive action against Iranian attacks. In his speech at the conference in Birmingham, Cartlidge will say: "With a £10bn budget, this would be one of Britain's most significant military programmes since the cold war. "But one that is totally necessary because of the threats we face." Streeting said in response: "They [the Conservatives] cut the Army to its smallest size since Napoleon and left a £17 billion hole in the equipment plan. "Their own defence secretary, Ben Wallace, admitted our Armed Forces had been 'hollowed out and underfunded'." The Conservatives said their plan would be funded within their existing commitment to spend 3% of GDP on defence by 2030, paid for by welfare reform and reprioritisation of existing expenditure. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has been under pressure to set out how he will reach Nato's 3.5% of GDP spending target by 2035, up from an estimated 2.6% this year. The current Labour government's Defence Investment Plan includes more than £350m to double the number of Sky Sabre systems operated by the British Army, with ground-based air defence sitting alongside air and maritime capabilities. Shadow ministers unveiled a series of policies on day two of the Conservative Party conference in Birmingham. Ahead of the Conservative conference, leader Kemi Badenoch says Labour has not been good for London. The Tory leader seeks to echo Margaret Thatcher as she sets out her guiding political principles. title: Author and former politician Jeffrey Archer dies aged 86
content: Bestselling author and former politician Jeffrey Archer has died at the age of 86. Archer sold more than 300 million books in his five-decade writing career, including the Clifton Chronicles and Kane and Abel, and often set the novels in his home town of Wellington, Somerset. In a statement, Archer's publisher HarperCollins said the author died "suddenly and peacefully at home" on Monday between writing sessions. The former Conservative MP was jailed for perjury in 2001 after being found guilty of lying and cheating in his 1987 libel case against the Daily Star. Archer was born in north London on 15 April 1940 but would quickly move to Weston-super-Mare in Somerset, where his family bought a house from John Cleese's mother. In 1969, Archer was elected MP for the Lincolnshire constituency of Louth. He served as an MP for five years before becoming Conservative Party deputy chairman. His political career was paused in 2001 when he was jailed for four years for perjury and perverting the course of justice. He was found to have lied in libel action he had brought against The Star newspaper, in which he was awarded £500,000 in damages. He was released in 2003 and returned to the House of Lords until he retired in 2024. His last book, Adam and Eve, is set to be released this week, HarperCollins said, describing him as a "master storyteller" whose readers "meant everything to him". The publisher added that the author had been at the Leicester Square Theatre in London on Sunday, signing books for fans with broadcaster Gyles Brandreth. Writing on X, Brandreth said: "Just yesterday I did a show with Jeffrey Archer to celebrate his new novel – he said it was to be his last. "He was in the most wonderful, ebullient form and had such a great reception from a packed house. He was funny, engaging and self-deprecating – a great storyteller to the last." Last week, Archer also returned to his former school to promote his last book. "It's wonderful to come back. What I got a real thrill about when I was walking towards the library is seeing the young boys and girls and thinking, 'that's the next generation'," Archer said at Wellington School. Archer was due to attend the Cheltenham Festival on Saturday to discuss his final novel. He and his wife Mary had celebrated their 60th wedding anniversary this year, HarperCollins said. The pair have two sons and five grandchildren. Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch described Archer's death as a "huge shock". Writing on X, she said: "I am incredibly saddened to hear this news. He had sent me a lovely message just this morning and was always a great source of encouragement to me personally." Paying tribute to the bestselling author, Kate Elton, HarperCollins UK CEO and Jeffrey's editor, said: "It has been one of the great privileges of my publishing life to have been Jeffrey Archer's editor. "He was the master storyteller and an editor's dream - phenomenally hard-working, utterly committed to completing draft after draft to get every word as perfect as possible, and a true champion of the 'team' nature of great publishing." Former Conservative chancellor Nadhim Zahawi paid tribute to the bestselling author on X, describing him as a "dear friend and extraordinary human being". He wrote: "His gift for storytelling was matched by his wit, warmth and boundless energy. Life was never dull in Jeffrey's company." She is hoping Edie's Magic Hair can be distributed to hospitals to help other children losing their hair. Kennington residents fundraise for the much-needed resource which will open on 10 October. Releasing next week, the latest take on Stephen King's novel has been criticised for its casting. The heroine is a softer, more conventional-looking character than in the book. Devon County Council hopes the change will encourage more people to borrow books. Nadia Shireen says people from South Asian backgrounds were not expected to become authors. Copyright 2026 BBC. title: Jeffrey Archer: successful novelist, disgraced politician and convicted liar
content: As many have observed, Jeffrey Archer, who has died aged 86, led a life as colourful as the plot in one of his novels. He was, at one time or other, a senior Conservative politician, a best-selling author, a peer of the realm, and a convicted perjurer. Possessed of huge drive, vast wealth and immense personal charm, Archer bounced back from disaster and, more than once, rebuilt a shattered life. But for all his talents, he will be remembered as a man affected by a defective moral compass, whose public humiliation was entirely self-inflicted. Jeffrey Howard Archer was born in north London on 15 April 1940. Within two weeks, his parents moved to Weston-super-Mare in Somerset, where they bought a house from John Cleese's mother. Archer's mother Lola was the first woman journalist on the weekly paper, the Weston Mercury. In later life, Archer insisted that his father William, who was some 40 years older than his mother, was a decorated hero of the First World War. In fact, he was a convicted fraudster who, according to a US newspaper, spent the war years conning people in New York. In 1951, the young Archer went to Wellington School on the edge of Exmoor. Some people mistakenly assumed he had gone to the somewhat more prestigious Wellington College in Berkshire, and he did little to correct them. Archer's academic career was undistinguished, and he left school with three O-levels. He did, however, embark on a fitness regime designed to improve his physique after his originally skinny frame led to taunts from fellow pupils. After school, he drifted. There was a brief spell in the army and then a short course in physical education in America. On his return, he spent five months as a probationary constable in the Metropolitan Police, before quitting to become a physical training instructor at a small prep school in Hampshire. It was while holding a similar job at Dover College that his resume moved into the realms of fantasy. He styled himself Jeffrey Archer, FIFPC, BSc, leading people to assume he had obtained a degree during his time in the United States. In fact, as his unofficial biographer Michael Crick later discovered, Archer's alma mater in the States was, in fact, a bodybuilding club. However, Dover College was so impressed, it backed Archer's bid to go to Oxford as a mature student to do a one-year Diploma of Education course. At Oxford, he excelled in athletics, winning a Blue, although it was doubtful whether his course qualified him to be a bona fide member of the University. More importantly, it brought him into contact with fellow students who would go on to hold senior positions in politics, finance and the media. He also married Mary Weeden, a chemistry student whose beauty had attracted a long list of suitors. "It was love at first sight for me," the future novelist recalled, "but I don't think it was for her." His public profile had been considerably raised when he managed to persuade The Beatles to come and support a £500,000 fundraising effort for Oxfam, a charity which Archer supported. After serving as a Conservative councillor in London, he was put on the selection list for the safe Tory seat of Louth in Lincolnshire. A reporter on the Times, John Clare, discovered that another charity for which Archer worked alleged he had misused expenses with claims for meals at posh London restaurants. Clare buttonholed Archer and, according to his own account, the would-be candidate burst into tears and asked that the story be quashed. It eventually appeared in the paper but with many of the salient details left out. Concerns about Archer's suitability were ignored by the party members in Louth who adopted him. In a by-election in December 1969, he won the seat with a handsome majority. He and Mary set themselves up in an expensive Kensington house and he became a member of Lloyds. He also began to build up his profile in parliament where he was seen as a liberal member of his party. But, in 1974, he suffered a blow after being persuaded to invest in a Canadian company which claimed to have developed a process to cut carbon emissions. It turned out to be a scam. Archer had taken out a second mortgage, as well as borrowing large sums from elsewhere, to raise money for the investment. Threatened with bankruptcy, he was forced to quit his parliamentary seat. However, he managed to secure an agreement with his creditors and wrote his first novel, Not a Penny More, Not a Penny Less in 1976. Charting an American immigrant's rise from messenger boy to corporate tycoon, it was inspired, in part, by his own financial problems and did much to solve them. Despite being rubbished by many critics, it sold well in the US and then in Britain, earning Archer a considerable sum in royalties. Three years later, Kane and Abel, a ripping page-turner about the roller-coaster financial fortunes of two men who initially shared nothing but a date of birth, flew off the shelves. A third novel, published in 1984, First Among Equals, about a cutthroat competition to become Prime Minister, cemented Archer's position as one of Britain's best-selling and highest earning authors. It enabled him to purchase the Old Vicarage at Grantchester near Cambridge, formerly the home of war poet, Rupert Brooke, as well as a penthouse in London. There, he entertained the great and the good with legendary parties, serving with champagne and shepherd's pies. First Among Equals, with its political theme, had more than hinted at Archer's desperation to get back into politics. He got his chance in 1985, when Margaret Thatcher, impressed by his drive and personality, gave him an unpaid job as Deputy Chairman of the Conservative Party with responsibility for fundraising. It lasted just a year. In October 1986, the News of the World published a picture of Archer's friend, Michael Stackpole, paying £2,000 to a sex worker named Monica Coghlan. The money was supposedly a bribe to persuade her to go abroad, to avoid the prying eyes of the press. And while the News of the World did not allege Archer had slept with Coghlan, the Daily Star was less reticent. Archer resigned his party post and sued the Star for libel. In court, he claimed the payment had been a goodwill gesture to a woman down on her luck. Friends also gave him an alibi for the night the Star had claimed he was enjoying the company of Ms Coghlan. It was the evidence of Mary Archer that swung the case. Her appearance in court so captivated the judge, Mr Justice Caulfield, that in his summing up, he asked why a man with such a fragrant wife would sleep with prostitutes. "Is he in need of cold, unloving, rubber-insulated sex," Caulfield asked, "in a seedy hotel round about quarter to one on a Tuesday morning after an evening at the Caprice?" The jury duly found for Archer and he was awarded £500,000 in damages. The News of the World later settled out-of-court with him, admitting they too had libelled him. He went back to writing his books which continued to sell. By this time, he was thought to be worth more than £50m. In 1992, he was offered a peerage by Conservative Prime Minister John Major in recognition for his work with a charity set up to help Kurds who were being oppressed by Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein. His wife, meanwhile, had joined the board of Anglia Television which, in 1994, was the subject of a takeover bid. The day after the move was discussed by the board, Archer bought 50,000 shares in the company on behalf of a friend. When the news of the takeover broke, the shares climbed in value and Archer made a profit of nearly £78,000. A subsequent investigation cleared him of insider dealing, but soured relations with the Conservatives who were mired in their own battle against allegations of sleaze. Undeterred, Archer, with the support of new Conservative leader William Hague, was selected as the Conservative candidate for Mayor of London in 1999. Once more, the threat of scandal forced his resignation when the News of the World printed an interview with Archer's former friend, Ted Francis. Francis alleged that the politician had lied on oath in his 1987 libel action against the Daily Star and Archer resigned as Conservative candidate for Mayor the next day. There would be no forgiveness. "This is the end of politics for Jeffrey Archer," said William Hague. "I will not tolerate such behaviour in my party." In 2000, Archer was charged with perjury and perverting the course of justice. At the same time, his play, The Accused, opened in London. It featured a murder in which the audience were the jury and decided the guilt, or otherwise of the protagonist at the end of each performance. In May 2001, a month after Monica Coghlan's death in a road accident, Archer went on trial. This time, his wife's testimony failed to sway the court. He was convicted and sentenced to four years in prison. Shortly after his conviction, police began investigating allegations of corruption. These related to the Kurdish charity in which Archer had been involved. There had been complaints that much of the £57m he said he'd raised never reached the Kurds. However, police concluded that Archer, in fact, had received very little of the donations himself. First in HM Prison Belmarsh and then in HM Prison Weyland, Archer used his incarceration profitably - by writing a three-volume account of his time inside entitled My Prison Diary. Two years later, he was released, having served half of his sentence. "I learned a lot from it," he said. "The British people are very forgiving." He retained his seat in the House of Lords, as there was no mechanism to remove an errant peer. He remained a member of Britain's upper house until his formal retirement in 2024. Writing well into his mid-80s, he continued to churn out at least one, if not two, novels a year. In the last years of his life, there were several volumes of The Clifton Chronicles: detailing the turbulent life of former dockworker, Harry Clifton. There were also seven novels about a fictional policeman, William Warwick, who rises from humble constable in the Metropolitan police to the very top of his profession. In January 2026, the 85-year-old announced that his forthcoming novel, Adam and Eve, would be his last. An epic tale inspired by Hitler's indecision about whether to invade Britain, Archer poured everything into it. "Everyone would like to run their last 100m at the Olympics and win the gold medal," he told BBC Breakfast in September 2026. Few critics praised Archer's prose style, his sense of humour, or the emotional depth of his characters. But none could match his talent for relentless, aspirational, rags-to-riches plots that, once started, could not be put down. Lord Archer often appeared incapable of separating autobiographical fact from fantasy in his continuing drive for public recognition. He died a wealthy man, albeit one whom very few trusted. title: 'Not again': Arrest of US marine for murder reignites protests in Japan's Okinawa
content: For many Okinawa locals, the arrest of a US soldier accused of robbing and killing a woman in a hotel room has reignited decades of frustration over crimes involving US military personnel there. "Honestly my first reaction was, 'Not again,'" 52-year-old longtime Okinawa resident Ai Sato told the BBC. "Nothing has changed since I was a child. How many times are we going to repeat the same thing, create more victims, cause their families to suffer, and ultimately, cause the people of Okinawa to grieve?" Akemi Oshiro, a 62-year-old Ginowan resident shared similar sentiments. "I know we shouldn't get used to terrible things like this, but because they keep happening, I've stopped being surprised," she told the BBC. Okinawa hosts the largest US military presence in Japan. It is home to several US military bases and tens of thousands of American troops. US Marine Lance Corporal Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, was arrested by Japanese police on Sunday. Police say an investigation is underway and that Ballard is in Japanese custody because the alleged crime was unrelated to official military duties. Whether a US service member is acting in the performance of official duty or not can determine which country has primary jurisdiction. When Japan has jurisdiction, but the suspect is under US custody, they can retain custody until Japan brings charges. Ballard was assigned to III Marine Expeditionary Force and stationed at Marine Corps Air Station Futenma in Ginowan City. The Okinawa prefectural police say 39-year-old Anna Yagi was found dead early 3 October in a hotel room in Naha. Security footage allegedly shows a man believed to be the suspect entering the hotel with the woman and leaving alone with her belongings. Local media citing police have reported that Yagi appeared to have been strangled with a cord. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi registered an official protest with Washington. But residents like Sato feel that's far from enough. "I am deeply disappointed by the same kinds of government comments we have been hearing for decades -- that they will protest or that they take the matter seriously." "I want Prime Minister Takaichi to call President Trump directly, someone with whom she has been emphasizing as having a close relationship with, and discuss concrete measures to prevent this from happening yet again," she said. Following news of the suspected murder, people in Japan have been voicing anger with some 100 people protesting in both Naha and Tokyo. Others took to social media expressing their outrage and demanding justice with one user saying: "Enough is enough." Over the past few years, a number of accidents and crimes have led to growing local opposition to the US presence on the island. The 2016 rape and murder of a 20-year-old local woman saw tens of thousands of protesters demonstrate against the heavy US presence there. A former US marine subsequently received a life sentence for the crime. The US currently has about 55,000 military personnel stationed in Japan, with the heaviest concentration based on the tropical island prefecture. Okinawa is one of the country's smallest prefectures by size, but 70% of the land used exclusively by the US military in Japan is located there. In 1972, Okinawa prefecture was returned to Japanese control after United States forces occupied the islands at the end of the Second World War. Since then, there have been 6,409 arrests for criminal offenses related to US military personnel, according to Okinawa Prefectural Government. Locals say the significant US presence has stirred resentment over a number of issues from crimes including rapes, assaults, and drunk-driving accidents to local disturbances such as noise and aircraft crashes. In 1995, three US servicemen abducted, beat, and raped a 12-year-old schoolgirl as she walked home from a stationery store. In 2025, a US Marine was convicted of choking and sexually assaulting a Japanese woman. "Even 80 yeas after the war, Okinawa where we live is a place that is so unnerving," 48-year-old mother of two boys Hitomi Miyagi told the BBC. "We will not stop raising our voices hoping for an Okinawa, where we can live in peace." Anojan Sivarasa faces execution after he was found guilty of blasphemy over a Facebook comment. Caleb Flynn, a former music pastor from Ohio, fatally shot his wife Ashley in February before trying to cover it up. Police in Baltimore have said the young girl was not a target of the shooting but was caught in the crossfire. The convicted killer is in hospital in Tennessee after surviving two lethal injections, in a case that has raised many questions. title: A simple guide to the US midterms
content: There are four weeks to go until the US midterm elections, when voters take part in a ballot that could have a major impact on the rest of Donald Trump's presidency. On 3 November, Americans will choose members of Congress, which is made up of two parts - the House of Representatives and the Senate. Elections take place every two years, and when they happen in the middle of the president's four-year term of office, they are called the midterms. A key task of Congress is to create and pass federal laws - laws that apply nationwide. The outcome of the midterms will decide which political party - Trump's Republicans or opposition Democrats - controls Congress and how easy it is for the president to carry out his plans. The results are also seen as a measure of how happy people in the US are with the president's performance so far. All 435 members of the House - the lower chamber of Congress - will be elected. They serve fixed terms of two years. The House is where proposed laws are introduced and debated. Meanwhile, 35 of 100 seats in the Senate, the upper chamber, will also be up for grabs. Senators serve six-year terms. Among other jobs, they approve or block proposed laws that have been received from the House. On the same day, voters across much of the US will also choose state-level politicians. Governor contests in California, Florida, Georgia and Michigan will be among the most closely watched. The US economy is on the minds of many voters struggling with the price of fuel, groceries, housing and healthcare. Inflation remains above the level targeted by the US Federal Reserve, partly down to the war that the US and Israel started with Iran in February. Democrats argue Trump's programme of trade tariffs have also pushed up prices for Americans. Immigration is another key issue. Republicans say Trump has delivered on a major campaign pledge in 2024 by tightening the border and launching a widespread - and often controversial - crackdown on illegal immigration. Concerns over AI have grown in urgency in recent weeks. Senior politicians from both parties have agreed on the need to regulate it - setting themselves in opposition to Trump, who has rejected the idea of laws to control development of the technology. Congress is one of the three branches of government, alongside the presidency and the judiciary. Control of it matters for the shaping of legislation. Both the House and Senate are currently held by the Republican Party. But its majority is a slender one. They have 218 seats in the House, which is the minimum number needed to control it, plus one independent who votes with them. In the Senate, they have 53 seats and the minimum needed for control is 51. If opposition Democrats win back control of at least one chamber, they will gain power to bring their own laws to the floor. Voters have tended to "punish" the party of the president in the past and vote against them. Recent polling shows a low approval rating for the president. He began his second term as president with an approval rating of just over 50%, according to polling resource website Silver Bulletin, but in early October it was sitting at about 37%. Meanwhile 61% disapproved of him. But not all seats in each chamber are competitive. Some are a safe bet for Republicans or Democrats. The BBC's US partner CBS News has identified nine Senate races to watch , in states like Iowa and New Hampshire, and 42 House races, in states like Arizona and Ohio. The vote is more unpredictable this year because of a battle between the two parties over the way voting districts in the House of Representatives are drawn. Republicans tried to gain an advantage by creating more favourable electoral maps in certain states and Democrats followed suit. If the Democrats win either the House or the Senate then Trump will find it difficult to get any laws through Congress. So his domestic plans could be frustrated, although he has found ways to exercise power without his wider party. Democratic control of either chamber would also mean they could use committees to investigate aspects of the Trump presidency. Corruption allegations, the new White House ballroom and ICE tactics could be subject to scrutiny. There is also a debate within the Democratic Party about whether to impeach Trump, which means to bring charges in Congress that will form the basis for a political, not criminal, trial. If the Republican Party stays in control of Congress, Trump will be able to keep going with his plans for the remainder of his time in office. The president's name is not on the ballot during the midterm elections, though Trump has urged Republicans to pretend that it is by voting for him as an endorsement of his actions so far. Whichever way the results fall, commentators are likely to use them to make arguments about how voters feel about the direction of the country under Trump's leadership. Trump cannot run to be president a third time. After the midterms, we can expect speculation to start building about who might be his successor as the Republican presidential nominee for 2028 - and who might compete against that person for the Democrats. The Pentagon confirmed on Sunday it had removed the B1 bombers from the base in England back to their home stations in America. The Pentagon confirmed on Sunday it had removed its bombers - thought to be about a dozen B-1s - from the base back to their home stations in America. It labelled Anthropic a "supply chain risk" in February after the firm refused to remove safety guardrails from its tools. The US president said his national intelligence chief will lead the group as worries over AI grow. Polls suggest the election will be a closely run contest between the left-wing incumbent and his right-wing rival. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: King's funding for Andrew not to be used for legal action against police
content: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has been told that the allowance given to him by King Charles should not be used to fund his legal action against Thames Valley Police and the Central Criminal Court. The King uses his own private money to support his brother and to accommodate him on his estate in Sandringham. But a royal source said that this funding should not be used for a legal challenge being launched by Mountbatten-Windsor against the search warrants issued ahead of his arrest in February. The former Prince Andrew was arrested on suspicion of misconduct in public office in the wake of information that emerged from the Epstein files in the United States. Mountbatten-Windsor has consistently denied any wrongdoing linked to his association with Epstein. The former Prince Andrew is not a working royal - so Buckingham Palace no longer speaks on his behalf and is not involved in his legal battle. But a royal source said the King's financial support for his brother should not be directed towards paying for the judicial review that Mountbatten-Windsor is seeking. It's not been disclosed how much the King gives to Mountbatten-Windsor, but the funding for his brother was part of the arrangement when the former Prince Andrew was moved from his previous home at Royal Lodge in Windsor. This allowance for Mountbatten-Windsor is not from the Sovereign Grant, which is the £138m in public funding for the monarchy. It is drawn from the King's private money, which includes his income from the Duchy of Lancaster, private estates and his own investments and inheritances. At the time of Mountbatten-Windsor's arrest, the King said the "law must take its course", and the Palace is now distancing itself from the former Duke of York's legal pushback. Mountbatten-Windsor's lawyers are understood to be challenging Thames Valley Police and the Central Criminal Court over the lawfulness of warrants used for searches of Sandringham and Royal Lodge - in what has been Andrew's first public response since his arrest earlier this year. Thames Valley Police has confirmed it is "engaged in legal proceedings in relation to warrants previously obtained from the Central Criminal Court". It added: "As these legal proceedings are currently ongoing, it would be inappropriate for us to comment further." Mountbatten-Windsor, who lost his titles as a prince and Duke of York over his connections to the sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, wants a judicial review to consider the legality of the search warrants. A court hearing on Thursday afternoon will be part of Mountbatten-Windsor's bid to quash the warrants. The warrants had been issued by a judge at the Central Criminal Court on 18 February - the day before Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested in Sandringham. "Even if Andrew succeeds in having the search warrants quashed, that would not necessarily be the victory it might first appear," said Nick Vamos, a criminal lawyer at Peters & Peters and former head of special crime at the Crown Prosecution Service. Vamos said disputes over warrants were not uncommon - but if the police lost on a technical error, they could still sometimes keep what they had obtained in a search. "The police can apply back to the Crown Court to retain the material if they have grounds to immediately seize it again," said Vamos. It would need to be a more fundamental issue with the granting of the warrants for the police to be required to return the material from a search, he said. Mountbatten-Windsor's arrest, carried out on his 66th birthday, followed a series of revelations from the Epstein files, published by the US Department of Justice. They included emails appearing to show official documents being shared by Mountbatten-Windsor with Epstein and others, at a time when he was the UK's trade envoy. Mountbatten-Windsor had already been stripped of his titles by King Charles, after emails had shown Mountbatten-Windsor had continued his links with Epstein, beyond when he had publicly said connections had been severed.
