title: Yemeni military says it has 'secured' Red Sea waterway
content: Yemeni pro-government forces backed by Saudi Arabia say they have "secured" the Bab al-Mandab Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea, at the start of a major offensive against the Iran-backed Houthi movement. The Yemeni military also said in a statement that National Shield, Giants Brigades and Tihama Resistance forces had captured the Red Sea city of Mokha on Monday afternoon with the help of Saudi air strikes. But in conflicting reports, unnamed Yemeni government and military sources told news agencies Reuters and AFP that the forces have only reached the city's outskirts. There was no immediate comment from the Houthis regarding Mokha. Four government sources told Reuters that Yemeni forces had reached the outskirts of Mokha late on Monday, and that Houthi fighters were now retreating. Government military sources who spoke to AFP would not confirm the capture of the city, but said "our forces took control of the Dhubab military airfield and cut the road linking the Dhubab district to the Bab al-Mandab area". Earlier, the Yemeni military also said its forces had seized Dhubab airport, 45km (27 miles) to the south, and were besieging Houthi fighters inside the nearby town. Houthi-run media denied reports that government forces had also made advances in Dhubab. The government said operations had also begun on other fronts on Monday, including the capital Sanaa, which fell to the Houthis at the start of the civil war 12 years ago. Meanwhile, a Saudi-led military coalition said its fighter jets were providing "round-the-clock" air support to the pro-government forces and had destroyed 324 "high-value" targets since the start of the offensive. Saudi air strikes killed a schoolgirl and a woman in the Sanhan and Saawan districts of Sanaa on Monday, according to Houth-run Al Masirah TV. Houthi spokesman Mohammed Abdul Salam said Saudi Arabia was committing "dozens of massacres" and that it must "bear all the consequences". The Houthi-run Humanitarian Operations Co-ordination Centre warned civilian airlines that Saudi airspace, except for the skies above the Islamic holy cities of Mecca and Medina, was no longer safe because it had become "a theatre of operations". On Sunday, the head of Yemen's internationally recognised Presidential Leadership Council announced the beginning of an offensive, dubbed Operation Yemen Dawn, aimed at retaking all territory held by the Houthis. Rashad al-Alimi insisted that all opportunities for de-escalation had been exhausted and called on all forces to carry out their assigned missions "until the country is liberated from the grip of the Houthi terrorist militia". It came after the Houthis reportedly cut a mountain road near the south-western city of Taiz, effectively leaving government forces and residents there surrounded. The Houthis also said they had launched ballistic missiles and drones at oil facilities belonging to Saudi Aramco in Riyadh and the Khurais area of Saudi Arabia in retaliation for dozens of Saudi strikes on their territory. According to BBC Verify, satellite imagery from Saturday shows thick, dark smoke coming from the site of a strike at the Aramco Riyadh Refinery, in the city's south-east. A similar plume of smoke can be seen rising from the Khurais Central Processing Facility as well as from a potential strike point in satellite imagery from Sunday. Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule. A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom. Last month, the Houthis launched a surprise offensive along Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast and quickly ousted pro-government forces from areas overlooking the Bab al-Mandab Strait, including Mokha, Dhubab and Perim (Mayyun) Island. They said they posed no threat to international shipping passing through the waterway but that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia. However, the seizure of the strait contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf. At least 959 people have been killed and 5,000 injured in the fighting in Yemen since 6 August, according to the government's health ministry. The UN says another 197,000 people have been displaced. title: Blue Planet and Gandhi composer George Fenton dies aged 76
content: Composer George Fenton, whose work included music for films such as Gandhi, Groundhog Day and The Fisher King, as well as TV shows like Planet Earth and Bergerac, has died at the age of 76. The prolific musician received five Oscar nominations for his film scores, including those for The Remains of the Day and Cry Freedom. His work on the BBC TV show Blue Planet also earned awards from the Baftas, Emmy Awards and Ivor Novellos; and he also composed theme music for BBC News programmes such as Newsnight and Breakfast Time. In a statement, Fenton's family said: "We are very sad to announce that George Fenton passed away unexpectedly today." They continued: "He is survived by his loving wife Amanda, ex-wife Jane, children Gemma, Grace and Bridget, and grandchildren Lola, Audrey, Alfred, George, Frank and Beatrice, and a life of music." Fenton was born George Howe in Bromley, Kent in 1949. According to a biography on his official website, his father was a mechanical engineer, and his mother had been a dancer before becoming a nurse during the war. Both parents were musical - his father played drums and his mother played piano - but Fenton chose the electric guitar as his instrument at the age of seven. That was "when music became more important than football," he later told The Express newspaper. "The Beatles had a huge influence on me." He took his first lessons from a musician called Brian Rudd. "He came into our lives as a chimney sweep, which he clearly wasn't," Fenton later recalled. "My mother went mad at him because he filled the house with soot. "As he left he said, 'I'm really sorry – but I tuned the boy's guitar for you.' She suggested that as compensation for the mess he could give me a lesson, which he did and then carried on doing." Later, Fenton began to study the church organ, but rejected the chance to attend university and music college to pursue a career as a performer. In 1968, he appeared in Alan Bennett's first West End play Forty Years On and was forced to adopt his mother's maiden name, as union rules prevented two actors from having the same name. During that production, he also understudied the musical director of the show, Carl Davis - who similarly became a prominent composer for film and television. A year later, he signed a record deal, and scored a top 10 hit in Sweden with a cover of The Beatles' Maxwell's Silver Hammer, but his career as a solo artist was short lived. In the mid-1970s, he had a recurring role as soldier Martin Gimbel in the ITV soap opera Emmerdale Farm. But as time went on, he found that directors were always casting him in roles that required him to play an instrument, so he decided to make music his main focus. Fenton got his first job as composer and musical director for a production of Twelfth Night at the Royal Shakespeare Company in Stratford-upon-Avon in 1974. Eight years later, he was nominated for an Oscar for his score for Richard Attenborough's Gandhi, on which he worked with Indian composer and instrumentalist Ravi Shankar to develop a score reflecting the country's musical traditions. It was only his fourth attempt at film music, and he was still almost entirely self-taught. Throughout the 1980s, he wrote the soundtrack for a number of TV series, including the Bafta-winning The Jewel in the Crown, The Monocled Mutineer, and Alan Bennett's Talking Heads. He also wrote many well-known theme tunes, including the BBC's One O'Clock News, Six O'Clock News, Nine O'Clock News, Newsnight, The Money Programme, and Radio 4's PM Programme. For 1987's Cry Freedom - the story of South African campaigner Steve Biko, who was brutally killed by police - he worked with South African jazz musician Jonas Gwangwa, earning two Oscar nominations for best original score and song. Almost by accident, the title track featured Fenton singing a list of anti-apartheid activists imprisoned or killed by the South African government. He'd initially recorded the lyrics as a guide for Gwangwa - but the musician decided to keep some of them intact "as a gesture of brotherhood". "Then it got nominated for an Oscar, so I then found myself singing it on live television to about a billion people, which was not what I intended at all," Fenton later told Radio 4's Desert Island Discs. After composing the score for the BBC's Trials of Life in 1990, Fenton went on to create the music for what became known as David Attenborough's Earth Trilogy: The Blue Planet, Planet Earth and Frozen Planet. Fenton's music perfectly complemented the stunning visuals of the ocean's depths and the polar ice caps, adding an emotional weight to the narrative, using the full might of the orchestra to evoke everything from wonder and awe to tension and suspense. Following the success of the documentaries, Fenton created a show - The Blue Planet in Concert - which has been performed by leading orchestras in venues around the world. Among his other well-known soundtracks were The Long Walk Home, You've Got Mail, Sweet Home Alabama, The Lady In The Van and Mrs Henderson Presents. Fenton also scored more films for British director Ken Loach than any other composer. Their 18 collaborations included Ladybird, Ladybird; I, Daniel Blake and The Wind That Shakes the Barley, which won the Palme d'Or at the 2006 Cannes Film Festival. He also founded the Association of Professional Composers, which later merged with The Ivors Academy; and he is one of only a handful of musicians to receive the Academy's fellowship, alongside Sir Andrew Lloyd Webber, Sir Elton John, Kate Bush, Bruce Springsteen and George Michael. In addition, Fenton was a visiting professor at the Royal College of Music and the University of Nottingham. He was made a CBE for services to music in 2023. The composer often said that his musical career had been an accident, but nothing gave him greater joy than seeing his work come to life. On his episode of Desert Island Discs, Fenton chose one of his own compositions - Reunion, from the soundtrack to the movie Accidental Hero - as it reminded him of watching pianist John Lowe play the melody in the studio. "If I was sitting on a desert island and thinking about what a good time I'd had writing music, which I have, I want just one thing to remind me about the best part - which is the fact that you write something and then you're so surprised and thrilled at the way it's played," he told Sue Lawley. "For a composer, that's the biggest kick you can get." The star reveals why he is "very selective" about releasing music - and shares his future collab hopes. title: Pentagon stops using Anthropic AI tools after blacklisting company, BBC told
content: The US Department of Defence is no longer using Anthropic's AI tools, an official has told the BBC, months after it designated the company a supply chain risk on national security grounds. The Pentagon "has ceased the use of Anthropic products", the department official said in a statement on Monday. Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth labelled Anthropic a supply chain risk in February, and announced that the Pentagon would stop using it by late August. It is not clear why there has been a delay. Multiple people familiar with the matter told the BBC that as recently as last week Anthopic's Claude model was still being used by the department in research, analysis and intelligence gathering as well as in military operations against Iran. It was viewed as a critical tool for sorting through vast quantities of information, the people said. They include former US defence officials and contractors who have worked closely with the Pentagon specifically on AI. A spokesman for Anthropic declined to comment when asked about the Pentagon's statement. The details of the department stopping all use of Anthropic's tools have not been previously reported. The firm had been used by the US government and military since 2024 and was the first advanced AI company to have its tools deployed in government agencies doing classified work. But earlier this year, the Pentagon pressed it to remove its safety guardrails from Claude and give the military unfettered access to its AI products. When Anthropic refused, citing concerns of mass surveillance and autonomous weapons, Hegseth designated the company a "national security supply-chain risk" - a law typically reserved for companies based in countries that pose a threat to the US. Anthropic said the move was "unprecedented and unlawful" and has sued the Trump administration in an effort to overturn the designation. As this legal fight has played out in the courts, the Pentagon has signed contracts with other major tech companies, including Google, xAI and OpenAI. OpenAI tools have been more widely adopted in recent months in some military departments, according to two people familiar with AI use in the defence department The Pentagon's statement on Monday came in response to a question from the BBC about its use of Anthropic, after multiple people said in interviews that Claude was still being widely used. It was embedded in a larger data platform used by the Pentagon called Maven Smart System, multiple sources said. Maven, which is operated by Palantir, is the Pentagon's primary platform for organising intelligence and other data. Lauren Kahn, a senior research analyst at Georgetown's Center for Security and Emerging Technology said that because Claude was deeply integrated into Maven it would have been difficult to remove it quickly from the system. "The fact that it took the Pentagon until now to remove all use of Claude from across the system is indicative that these things are not just plug and play," she said. "Once they become integrated it can be painful to remove them," added Kahn, a former US defence official. The BBC spoke with defence contractors who specialise in AI and have worked closely with the Pentagon, as well as former US defence officials and others familiar with the Pentagon's use of artificial intelligence. Several spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to speak to the media. When Hegseth initially ordered Anthropic to be phased out of government, "there was concern with moving beyond Anthropic to OpenAI" and other tools, a former senior US defence official said. Hegseth set a six-month deadline to phase out Anthropic on 27 February, one day before the US and Israel attacked Iran. Pentagon employees continued to use Anthropic's Claude tools, including its powerful Mythos models, "throughout the whole period of the controversy" with the company, one of the people said. Claude was used in particular for intelligence gathering and analysis, including through Palantir's Maven system, several sources said. Palantir, a leading defence tech firm, was founded by the billionaire ally of President Donald Trump, Peter Thiel. Sources familiar with the way the technology is used said analysts and other defence officials rely on Maven to access and organise visual data, including satellite imagery and drone footage. The data was then fed into Claude and other large language models for tasks such as identifying potential military targets. Officials frequently used the technology when compiling one-page briefs that were passed up the chain of command, according to a source who was given a demonstration of Maven by Palantir earlier this year. Maven is also used by some US allies to share intelligence with the Trump administration. Anthropic's clash with the Pentagon comes as relations with the White House appear to be warming. Trump met with Anthropic boss Dario Amodei twice at the White House last week. After one of the meetings with Trump and other technology leaders, Amodei said he still had concerns about risks posed by AI. "How we address those risks is still under discussion," Amodei told reporters at the White House, as Trump stood by his side, but "if we work with the president, we can win safely". title: Former American Idol contestant sentenced to life in prison for murdering wife
content: A US man who once appeared on the TV talent competition American Idol has been sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole for murdering his wife. Caleb Flynn, 40, was found guilty last week after a short deliberation by the jury, which rejected his claim that an intruder broke into his Ohio home and shot his wife, Ashley Flynn, as she slept. He was also found guilty of eight additional charges, including aggravated murder and tampering with evidence. Letters from his two daughters were read in court during the sentencing hearing on Monday, pleading with him to finally admit his guilt and questioning why he killed their mother. Flynn, a former music pastor, fatally shot his wife, a 37-year-old teacher, in February before staging their home in Tipp City to appear as if someone had broken in through the garage. Flynn claims he was asleep when he heard gunshots and found his wife dead in bed after finding the garage door open. Their two children, ages 9 and 11, were also sleeping in the house at the time. His wife's sister, Kayla Keyt, read a victim impact statement saying the murder had caused his daughters to question their Christian faith and had "shattered a family who trusted you". One of his daughter's letters read: "Dear Daddy, I don't even know where to start. How could you do such a thing?" She also said: "Mommy was the perfect person... And then you chose to kill the only mother I ever had." The other daughter's letter began "Dear Caleb", rather than addressing him as her father, and asked him to "tell everyone what you did it and receive your outcome". "You made me feel like an idiot thinking I could trust you," his daughter said. She added that she continues to have faith in God, and that she will never visit her father in prison. Flynn sobbed loudly as the letters from his children were read. The sentencing hearing also included Flynn reading a statement expressing love for his family, apologising for unspecified "decisions" that he made, and again claiming that he did not kill his wife. "I made vows to Ashley on our wedding day. I failed those vows," he said. Judge Jeannine Pratt called Flynn an "extreme" risk to the public as she imposed her sentence. The murder verdict last week followed eight days of testimony, during which several incriminating text messages Flynn sent to his former mistress, Alleigha Botner, were read out and AI-generated songs were played that prosecutors said he made for her. Evidence presented during trial included police body camera footage and activity on Flynn's iPhone and Apple Watch from around the time of the murder when he claimed to have been sleeping. The prosecution also called dozens of witnesses, including Botner, whom he met while she was an intern at his church. Botner read aloud in court some of their 100,000 text messages, including one where Flynn wrote: "I was up until 4am last night crying, literally thinking of ways to kill her and not go to jail." In another message, he wrote: "I just want her dead and gone." Flynn did not testify during the trial, and his defence team called no witnesses. His lawyer, Patrick Mulligan, has said he plans to file a notice of appeal, telling reporters last week: "There's a lack of evidence on prior calculation and design." Mulligan argued that evidence of infidelity was not evidence of murder and questioned why Flynn was being accused of tampering with evidence because his gun could not be found. This gun, which had been kept in the console of his truck, has been missing since investigators arrived at the scene and found the truck's centre console open. Prosecutor Paul Watkins read a statement from Ashley Flynn's family in court after the verdict in September, saying: "Ashley loved Jesus with her whole heart." "She loved people," the statement continued. "Most of all, she loved being a Mum." Flynn briefly appeared on American Idol in 2013, saying that he loved his wife "more than anything". Police in Baltimore have said the young girl was not a target of the shooting but was caught in the crossfire. The convicted killer is in hospital in Tennessee after surviving two lethal injections, in a case that has raised many questions. US media reported a new threat led to the bombers being removed on Sunday, following an incident near the base last week. It labelled Anthropic a "supply chain risk" in February after the firm refused to remove safety guardrails from its tools. The Pentagon confirmed on Sunday it had removed its bombers - thought to be about a dozen B-1s - from the base back to their home stations in America. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: Niamh O'Brien, dancer and wife of Michael Flatley, dies at 52
content: Niamh O'Brien, a former lead performer in Lord of the Dance and the wife of Riverdance star Michael Flatley, has died at the age of 52. Announcing her death on social media on Monday, Flatley said his "heart is broken". "My gorgeous bride of twenty years has gone to the Lord in Heaven." O'Brien was a renowned Irish dancer who performed the lead role of Saoirse in the Lord of the Dance shows. Flatley described her as "the most loving mother, wife and person and our lives will never be the same without her". The couple had a son, Michael St James, who was born in 2007. A representative for Flatley said that O'Brien died peacefully at the Beacon Hospital in Dublin after an illness, Irish national broadcaster RTÉ reports. "The Flatley and O'Brien families are devastated by Niamh's sudden passing and have asked that their privacy be respected as they come to terms with this heartbreaking loss," said the representative. "They express their sincere gratitude to the doctors, nurses and staff at Beacon Hospital who cared for Niamh over the past few weeks, and to everyone who has offered their kindness and support to the family." The people captured in a celebrated photograph are reunited nearly 50 years later. Gold medallist Tabby Stoecker will swap gym kit for sequins when she takes to the dancefloor on Saturday. The programme's sessions have been designed and delivered by English National Ballet. Berna Akinal says the fitness-dance class can be a "release" from the difficulties in life. Evie Bradford will attend Lane Theatre Arts - Victoria Beckham is counted among its famous alumni. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: Karoline Leavitt joining Fox News as on-air contributor
content: Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt will join Fox News as an on-air contributor next month, weeks after stepping down from her prior role to spend more time focusing on her family. Fox News said in a statement that Leavitt “will provide political analysis and commentary” across Fox platforms in her new role, which begins November 1. Leavitt added in a statement provided by Fox that she would bring “the same energy and candor that defined my tenure, to Fox’s millions of viewers across their many platforms.” Leavitt, who hails from Atkinson, New Hampshire, moved back to the Granite State with her husband and two young children, a source familiar told CNN. The Fox News release also noted her move. The network agreed to build a studio in her home, the source added. She formerly resided in the Naval Observatory in Washington with her family as press secretary. Trump announced on August 12 that Leavitt was leaving the White House, and he has yet to name a replacement . The last press briefing was on September 3, led by Vice President JD Vance. When Leavitt was on maternity leave earlier in the year, Vance and other Cabinet officials hosted briefings on a rotating basis. Trump told reporters at the White House on Thursday, “We have a lot of people who want that job. I would say many of them are right here,” pointing at Fox News correspondent Peter Doocy. When asked who he’s looking for, Trump joked: “Maybe a guy like Peter.” Leavitt said she left her role as press secretary to devote more time to her two young children, something she said was difficult to achieve in a top post at the White House. She remains in the president’s orbit, however, working at the Trump-aligned MAGA Inc. super PAC. Leavitt recently spoke at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas and helped host the AI-powered America.gov website launch last week in DC. In recent weeks, Leavitt appeared on Fox News host Sean Hannity’s show and podcast. Another former Trump White House press secretary, Kayleigh McEnany, joined Fox News after her tenure at the podium during the preisdent’s first term.

title: Trump uses anti-transgender slur to attack South Carolina Senate nominee
content: President Donald Trump on Monday used an anti-transgender slur to attack Democratic South Carolina Senate nominee Dr. Annie Andrews, as he tries to push his handpicked GOP candidate, Sen. Darline Graham , over the finish line in the midterm election. “Annie ‘Trannie’ Andrews is running against our wonderful Darline Graham for the Senate in South Carolina,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post. He used a version of the slur three times in the post. Andrews did not reference Trump’s comments in a statement responding to his post, instead saying, “I’m in this race to fight for my patients, my three kids, and South Carolina.” “And I’m going to work with anyone to put South Carolina first, because lowering costs and making life better for families across our state is going to take all of us working together. If you care more about your bills than the politics in Washington, this campaign is for you,” she said. The president has taken a particular interest in that Senate race, pushing for Graham’s appointment after the sudden death of her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham — who the president considered a close friend. His MAGA Inc. PAC then spent more than $800,000 to push Darline Graham to victory in the GOP primary runoff, and Trump personally campaigned for her. Now, a state that seemed like a relatively safe GOP win has become a fresh test of Trump’s influence. Two weeks ago, the Cook Political Report listed the race as likely Republican, rather than solidly Republican. And Trump allies have told CNN they are worried about Graham’s polling. The president lavishly praised Darline Graham in the post. “For years my dear friend Lindsey would say that, ‘Darline is the finest, most reliable, and one of the smartest people I have ever known.’ He would then always add, ‘Also, the most loyal!’ Oftentimes I would be upset with Lindsey for saying this, because I thought I had all of those qualities,” Trump wrote. Republicans in the state have frequently criticized Andrews for her positions on transgender issues, including her past support for providing hormone treatment for children. Andrews has said she does not support gender-identity surgery for minors. This story has been updated with additional information.

title: Trump says he will pay for campaign-style ads himself after backlash over taxpayer-funded effort
content: President Donald Trump said Monday he will no longer use taxpayer money to fund a series of promotional television ads , announcing that he will instead pay for them with funds raised for MAGA, Inc., the pro-Trump super PAC. “The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money. This is a rather standard thing to do but, rather than doing that, although nothing will make them happy, I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc. MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN!” Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social . The reversal follows criticism of the administration’s multimillion-dollar television advertising effort, which Republicans and Democrats alike have questioned. The White House has defended the spots as public service announcements. As of Monday, at least an estimated $10.1 million in taxpayer dollars have been spent on the ads, according to a leading political ad-tracking firm, AdImpact. As of last week, the administration had created at least 13 campaign-style ads promoting Trump and his policies. Spots that have yet to air include three ads highlighting the US military and operations in Iran and Venezuela, one titled “God Made Trump” and another recapping the UFC fight Trump hosted at the White House. CNN obtained clips of 12 of the ads , ranging from 15 seconds to three minutes long, two of which have already aired. They appeared in a Dropbox account shared with CNN and run by LMD, the agency awarded the government contract for the ad buys. Each ad ends with the words “Paid for by the U.S. Government” at the bottom of the screen. Another ad, “Final Battle,” which is not in the Dropbox account, has also aired in recent weeks. While each of the ads has a different theme, many of them include imagery of the president and audio with positive reviews from news reports. They also include patriotic images — including the cap toss at a military graduation, fireworks over Mount Rushmore and military flyovers. Trump has personally driven the video ads, CNN previously reported , including helping select the imagery and footage, according to a source familiar with the matter. Two Trump advisers said the ads were being produced in-house by the White House video team, part of the communications office responsible for the administration’s public messaging, though at least one was produced by a pro-Trump meme group. Watchdog groups have said the ads mark a clear violation of appropriations law restricting the use of federal funding for propaganda or partisan communications, but it’s not clear if outside groups have standing to file a lawsuit. Though the ads have received bipartisan criticism, Congress — which groups said had the clearest lane to provide some accountability — did not act to block the ads ahead of the midterms. CNN’s Betsy Klein contributed to this report.

title: US removes all Air Force bombers from UK base following new threat
content: The United States moved all of its long-range bombers stationed in the United Kingdom back to their American home bases on Sunday after an unspecified new threat, officials said. It comes days after the British government arrested a number of individuals in connection with an alleged Iranian plot to target the UK airbase where the planes had been stationed. “We can acknowledge now that all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home stations in the United States,” one official told CNN. The statement did not include details on why the planes were moved. The source familiar called the latest threat a “real world incident.” It is unusual that the US military would move the bombers back to their home stations instead of deploying them to another base in the region, the official said. President Donald Trump also confirmed that a threat had prompted the move – though he did not specify what the threat was. “I think we can say that — I mean, they didn’t fly out by accident,” Trump said from the White House. “There were some threats, and rather than tempting the enemy, we’ll capture the enemy and beat the enemy. But why should we leave them there? So we moved them around a little bit.” Vice President JD Vance said Monday that the move was made “out of an abundance of caution,” suggesting it was a response to a potential threat from Iran even as he declined to detail the specific concerns. “I think that we’re going to be as careful as we possibly can be,” Vance told reporters. “We do feel with some confidence that the Iranians are, you know, they’re trying to do what the Iranian state has done for 49 years, which is engage in acts of terrorism against the United States and against a lot of other people as well.” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, downplayed the removal of the US bombers, saying he would not “directly tie” the planes’ redeployment to the alleged Iranian plot. “The only reason why you guys are focused on how many planes are at Fairford is because of the threat that happened last week. But it’s not unusual to see rotations happen and movement of assets to different parts of the world based on exercises, redeployments, people changing out and new people coming in, new planes coming in, old planes going out,” Rubio told reporters at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland on Monday. Rubio added that the United States had worked closely on security with the UK for a long time, including on the Fairford investigation. A Downing Street spokesperson said that the UK government would not comment on foreign nations’ military operations. Asked about safety concerns by residents living near the base, the spokesperson told reporters that the UK has “the tried and tested approaches to defend our bases around the country, but not just that, throughout the world.” The UK Ministry of Defense also declined to comment on the operations or capabilities of other nations. The Royal Air Force base at Fairford has been used to deploy US B-1 bombers involved in the war against Iran and is an operating location for US Global Strike Command, which is tasked with managing long-distance strikes. CNN national security analyst Alex Plitsas said it was likely several dozen bombers were stationed at Fairford, adding that it was unusual to move all the aircraft. “It speaks to the credibility and the seriousness of the threat overall to the base that we’re talking about,” he told Ben Hunte on CNN Newsroom. The relocation of the bombers comes amid the investigation into the alleged plot. British police on September 27 arrested five men on suspicion of terror and explosives offenses close to the airbase. The men – identified only as British nationals between the ages of 23 and 25 and from the London area – were quickly released on bail, with police confirming no explosives were found in three vans at the scene. Their release sparked criticism from Trump, who said “I wouldn’t have done that.” A 25-year-old British-Iranian dual national was also arrested on Thursday in connection with the alleged plot. US intelligence had been tracking planning by Iranian groups to target US assets at the airbase for weeks before the initial arrests of the five on suspected terrorism charges, according to multiple sources familiar. The planning involved efforts to use intermediaries to recruit local criminal groups to carry out an attack, according to one of the sources and another person briefed on the matter. CNN was unable to learn whether the men who have been arrested were specifically known to authorities prior to last weekend; one of the sources said the Iranian planning was being tracked at a higher level. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said last week there are “strong indications” Iran was involved in the incident. “We will say more in due course, but we can confirm our belief that we believe Iran to have played a part,” he told the BBC on Sept 30. Burnham’s remarks appeared to support the US’ assessment that the incident involved a foreign actor. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said “the hands of a foreign actor” were involved in the alleged plot but declined to provide details in an interview with Fox News last week. “I think it ties us to the reality here. We are dealing with elements in the world, and in the case of Iran for example, who have openly threatened to attack American interests globally,” he said. Meanwhile, Iran has denied any involvement in the incident, described the accusations as baseless and summoned the British ambassador in Tehran, Iranian state media reported Thursday. During the meeting, Iran’s Deputy Foreign Minister Majid Takht-Ravanchi reportedly urged London to revise what he called its “inappropriate approach” toward Tehran. This has been updated with additional details.

title: Trump approves firing squad for execution of Nidal Hasan for 2009 Fort Hood massacre
content: President Donald Trump has approved the use of a firing squad for the execution of Nidal Hasan who was convicted in the 2009 massacre at Fort Hood in Texas. The Pentagon announced Monday night that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth recommended death by firing squad for Hasan and Trump approved it. Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell posted on X that Hegseth will set the time and place of the execution for “the jihadist who opened fire on unarmed American soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009.” “He killed 13 people and wounded 32 others while shouting ‘Allahu Akbar’ during the attack,” Parnell said. “Judgement day for Hasan has finally come.” Hegseth replied to Parnell’s post, saying, “Justice.” This story is breaking and will be updated.

title: Takeaways from Supreme Court arguments in major climate change case against Big Oil
content: The Supreme Court appeared conflicted Monday about how it will resolve a lawsuit from a Colorado city that is attempting to hold two fossil fuel companies responsible for the impacts of climate change, though several conservative justices said they were concerned about the possibility of letting states wade into an area long controlled by the federal government. As they opened a new term with the most important climate change case to reach their docket in nearly two decades, the conservative justices asked especially probing questions for the city and county of Boulder, which wants billions of dollars to help mitigate the cost of fires, floods and public health impacts associated with a warming climate. They also asked tough questions of the two oil companies, ExxonMobil and Canada-based Suncor Energy. Dozens of other cities have filed similar suits against oil and gas companies. A decision is expected next year. Here’s what to know about the oral arguments: Justice Brett Kavanaugh, a conservative who at times finds himself siding with liberals in a majority, offered the clearest opposition to Boulder. At one point he mused that the approach the city and county had taken in the litigation would “bankrupt” not just oil companies but potentially other businesses as well. Exxon and Suncor argued that the regulation of carbon emissions is inherently a federal issue, since pollution can waft across state and international borders. Kavanaugh repeatedly latched onto that argument, calling attention to past precedents in which the Supreme Court seemed to agree. “We’re on a wall of precedent that says state tort law does not apply,” Kavanaugh said. “This court would be rightly accused of misleading Congress for decades on what the state of the law was,” if a majority was to conclude that states and cities could bring such suits against polluters. Chief Justice John Roberts seemed particularly concerned with the implications of letting each individual city and state sue. “Presumably, if you prevail, the next day a municipality in every single state will file a lawsuit — probably copy your pleadings — and then there’ll be at least 50 different cities,” Roberts, a conservative, asked the attorney for Boulder. “How would you think that will work out on the ground?” Kevin Russell, the lawyer for Boulder, countered that the court had never deferred to federal law before just because of the possibility that a state action “if copied in other states, could cause a lot of litigation.” But Roberts also seemed to be troubled with some of the most sweeping arguments embraced by Exxon and the Trump administration, which is backing the oil companies. “There are a lot of familiar situations where conduct outside of a state has broad effects in other states … and yet we allow the state courts in a particular state to bring litigation,” Roberts said at one point. “I guess I’m not quite sure what makes this situation different from all those other ones.” This is the latest in a series of high-profile appeals in which both liberal and conservative states are attempting to adopt policies in a vacuum of action from a gridlocked Congress. Groups supporting Exxon warned of “runaway” litigation in which states sue to try to set national policy in a range of other areas, from food production to pharmaceuticals to artificial intelligence. Boulder says its suit is similar to those filed by states in the 1990s over the harmful health effects of tobacco. That effort, based in part on an argument that the tobacco companies deceived consumers, led to a massive settlement. In the climate case, Boulder not only argues that Exxon and Suncor contributed to climate change but that also misled the public about the harmful effects of their product, fossil fuels. “I’m waiting to see the distinction,” Justice Elena Kagan, a member of the court’s liberal wing, told Kannon Shanmugam, the lawyer for the energy companies. “This is the same kind of lawsuit, against the same kind of actor for the same kind of harm. And I guess I’m not understanding how it is that the one would be preempted and the other is not.” When Shanmugam responded by arguing that the difference is partly because of how carbon emissions work, Kagan fired back by questioning how the oil companies concluded that federal law inherently superseded state law when it comes to carbon pollution. “Wow, where is the text for that?” Kagan said at one point, a not-so-veiled reference to the conservative wing’s focus on deciding cases based on the clear text of the law of the Constitution. “Where’s the support for that? Where’s the precedent for that? Where’s the anything for that?” Justice Samuel Alito wasn’t present in the ornate courtroom Monday as he recently recused himself from the case . His absence could have significant consequences. The 6-3 conservative high court has almost always sided against environmental claims in recent years, with Alito usually in the majority. If a majority of justices can’t coalesce around a decision, then Alito’s recusal creates the possibility of a 4-4 split. That rare outcome would uphold the decision by Colorado’s Supreme Court that allowed Boulder’s lawsuit to proceed. But it would set no precedent for other cases and also allow Exxon and Suncor to continue to fight in lower courts, potentially returning to the US Supreme Court in the future. Alito told Bloomberg News he felt it was “prudent” to recuse, given his holdings in energy stocks, but not required. The companies Alito holds, which include ConocoPhillips and Phillips 66, were not named parties in the dispute before the high court. Those companies’ bottom lines would almost certainly be affected by whatever the high court decides. Alito, meanwhile, was in the news this weekend as he took part in a series of interviews to promote a book publishing Tuesday. Of particular focus was Alito’s remark that he “thought about” retiring , though he made clear he feels he can still make a “valuable contribution.” Lurking in the climate case is a highly technical question that could prove to be an escape valve. Because of the way Colorado’s highest court resolved the dispute, the justices could also find a more limited way out of the case by deciding that it isn’t yet fully baked for Supreme Court review. That outcome would send the case back to state courts — at least for a while. It was an idea that Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, a liberal, repeatedly pressed. “We’re really early in this case,” Jackson told Shanmugam. “This is sort of premature from the standpoint of this court exercising its jurisdiction.” Shanmugam noted the companies are facing dozens of similar suits and said the federal questions raised need to be resolved “sooner rather than later.” One of Jackson’s colleagues who remained relatively quiet was Justice Clarence Thomas, a conservative. Thomas twice asked about the same issue as Jackson — whether the court should wait for a later stage of the litigation. But it was unclear what Thomas thought about that question. Thomas was highly cited in the written arguments for Boulder because the longest-serving current justice has in the past been skeptical of letting federal law trump state law in other areas, particularly when Congress has not clearly stated its intention to do so. “If you prevail, is there a limiting principle as to whom you can sue?” Thomas asked Russell. “So, you could just as easily sue large retailers of these products.” Alito rejoined the bench for the second case of the day, as the nine justices gathered for their first public appearance since late June, when they handed down major rulings rejecting President Donald Trump’s attempt to limit birthright citizenship and upholding a state’s ban on transgender athletes. Despite a busy summer with a series of emergency appeals dealing with the midterm election and Trump policies, the justices seemed to settle into the routine on Monday without incident. The courtroom was especially packed, and a small group of protesters gathered outside. Roberts briefly made the formal recognition that the 2025-2026 term was “now closed” and that the new term was “now convened.” Other major issues on deck this term include an important Second Amendment challenge to bans on AR-15 rifles , a fight over whether religious preschools receiving taxpayer money may decline to enroll the children of same-sex couples and a series of cases dealing with Trump’s immigration policies. And there will be more to come. The justices have granted less than half the caseload they’re expected to decide by June. The court may later this year take up a review of state laws requiring the Ten Commandments to be posted in public school classrooms. Meanwhile, a legal battle raging between prediction sites like Kalshi and Polymarket and state governments has already reached the justices. The court may also be called on to decide a flurry of emergency election cases in the final run-up to the November midterms or in the immediate aftermath. Those cases will almost require the court to move with unusual speed, drawing attention away from its regular merits docket. This story and headline have been updated with new details about oral arguments.

title: Green party of England and Wales facing international ostracism over ‘Zionism is racism’ vote
content: The English and Welsh Greens are facing international ostracism after adopting a policy declaring Zionism as a form of racism, which has drawn dismay from the group representing European Greens. The co-leader of the German Greens separately said the policy was “intolerable and unacceptable”, running contrary to its belief in the right of Israel to exist. The binding policy motion passed in a vote at the Greens’ conference in Brighton on Sunday. Four of the party’s five MPs opposed it. The policy says Zionism , the movement for a Jewish state, should be “treated as any other form of racism”, and backs a single democratic Palestinian state across historic Palestine “with equal rights for all”. The European Green party , which represents 47 parties, including the Green party of England and Wales (GPEW), said it supported a two-state solution for Israel and Palestine, and the new motion went against this. The alliance “will immediately demand clarity from the leadership and parliamentary group of GPEW, to understand the official party policy of GPEW, how they position themselves towards the self-determination of Israelis and Jews as well as the protection of Jewish people and members in the party”, it said in a statement. Felix Banaszak, the leader of the German Greens, known formally as Alliance 90/the Greens, told a press conference the motion was “intolerable and unacceptable”. “It runs counter to everything that Alliance 90/the Greens stands for in Germany , and it also runs counter to what the European Green party stands for,” he added. Banaszak said: “There is a widely held view within the European Green party that Israel has a right to exist and that this right must not be undermined.” His party would “approach our partner parties in Europe to clarify how to deal with this”. Sandy Ruthven, the chair of Amnesty International UK’s charitable trust and a longstanding Green member, resigned over the motion and accused the party of failing to confront antisemitism. The fallout from Sunday’s vote has also intensified a debate over whether the Greens’ highly decentralised policymaking structures remain suitable for a party whose membership has expanded rapidly. Policy is made at the party’s two annual conferences, which generally involve a small proportion of members. The Zionism motion won just over 1,000 votes, approximately 0.4% of the total membership. Ellie Chowns, a former co-leader, said the party’s governance and policymaking “urgently need to be modernised”. “As a party we pride ourselves on our democratic member-led policymaking process, but I do think we need to ask ourselves some searching questions when less than 1% of our members actually participate,” Chowns, the Green MP for North Herefordshire, told the Guardian. “This is long overdue and has become even more urgent with the huge expansion of our membership.” Chowns said she understood the concerns of European Greens, which she shared, but stressed: “There is still much more that unites us than divides us.” One source in the party said the criticism from European Greens, especially those in Germany, was understandable given their differing stances on Gaza and Israel. They said: “The German Greens support arming Israel, opposed a ceasefire to Israel’s onslaught on Gaza, backed the suspension of funding to Unrwa and co-sponsored a Bundestag resolution describing the arguments and methods of the peaceful, Palestinian-led BDS campaign as antisemitic.” Any change to internal party structures would be hard to implement. One Green insider said that to give MPs greater authority over members would undermine the party’s commitment to grassroots democracy. However, they said the existing model could produce a lack of coherence and strategic direction, while giving a disproportionate influence to members with the most time to participate in policymaking. They suggested members could determine broad strategic priorities, with smaller bodies developing detailed policy while remaining accountable to the membership. Another senior Green defended the party’s model of direct democracy, arguing that allowing members to determine policy was fundamental to the party’s character. Daniel Schuster, the regional director of the Simon Wiesenthal Center’s European office, said: “The British Green party’s decision to formally classify Zionism as a form of racism is absurd, not based on any logical basis and is itself racist. And timing, just days before the third anniversary of the 7 October terrorist Hamas attacks, is designed to inflict pain on a deeply solemn occasion. “Branding Zionism itself as racism crosses a profoundly consequential line. It takes a movement for Jewish national self-determination and transforms it into something for which Jews are expected to apologise. We will not.” In a statement, the Green party leader in England and Wales, Zack Polanski, said: “Antisemitism and criticism of the Israeli state are, and must always be, completely distinct – blurring the line between the two is not only wrong but antisemitic, and makes Jewish people less safe. It’s our role as a movement for justice to protect both the rights of Palestinians and our Jewish communities here in the UK. As leader I will not accept any exclusion, or refusal to engage with anyone, because of the religious or communal body they are part of.” He added: “Through the Green party’s unified stance and dedicated pressure, we have begun to shift this government away from its complicity with the Israeli government’s atrocities in Gaza, with the foreign secretary now taking the long overdue step of ending trade with illegal settlements.”

title: No queues, empty seats and the worst speech ever heard: welcome to the Tory conference
content: A t the Labour party conference in Liverpool last week, Andy Burnham floated the idea of electoral reform. This week in Birmingham, the Tories have come up with a plan of their own: voting with their feet. How to put this nicely? Let’s just say that the Conservative party conference is extremely civilised. No queues for the food concessions. No queues to get into any of the halls. In fact, the organisers are delighted that anyone has turned up at all. This doesn’t feel like a high-octane meeting of a party preparing for government. More like a home counties meeting of the Rotary Club. On current evidence, if there is a general election next year – as Kemi Badenoch is trying to convince us there will be – then the Tories won’t be active participants. More like vaguely disinterested observers. For these four days, Birmingham is a city where you can sit and watch the world pass you by. Not that those who have turned up seem unhappy. Rather, they are thrilled to find themselves still alive. This time last year, there was a possibility that they faced extinction: under threat from left and right and with a leader in Kemi who looked unlikely to last six months. Since then things have stabilised as Robert Jenrick has been stopped from pulling out their ventilator in the intensive care unit. They are now merely an endangered species. The conference centre is a safari park attraction where we get to see the remnants of the Tory party in a protected habitat. The morning’s activities take place in what is optimistically called the main hall: a hard-to-find side room with a capacity of about 200. These are way more seats than any of the acts require. First up was shadow transport secretary, Richard Holden, who managed to bore even himself. Still, at least the hall was about a third full. Which, for Rich, is a major result. I’m guessing most of the people there were family and friends. It was no fuller for the shadow health secretary, Damian Hinds, who stumbled over his notes for five minutes. Weirdly, there were 24 people watching an empty stage online after he had left, while only 17 had been online when he was talking. Or maybe that’s not so weird. For the afternoon offering we were moved to a slightly bigger hall. This could have been a mistake. It had come billed as a “major speech by the shadow chancellor”. Only we were made to sit through an hour and a half of nothingness – an opportunity to deliberate our own and the Tories’ existential futility – before the main event. By now at least another third of the audience had left. A wise choice. They clearly had some idea of what was coming. Even 20 minutes of Andrew Griffith can rip your soul in half. If only I had joined them. Not that the hall was anywhere near full to begin with. First up was the shadow Defra secretary, Victoria Atkins , who had sensibly worked out that no one in their right mind would stay to hear her talk. So instead she positioned herself as a cable TV presenter – there were 53 people watching online – chatting to her guest, Jeremy Clarkson. This did at least lift the mood in the hall. A genuine celeb was among them for 15 minutes. However, it doesn’t say much for your conference when your most popular speaker is someone who openly says he’s not a Tory party member and has only turned up because he will go anywhere people will have him to talk about farming. “Wow,” said Jezza. “There’s an awful lot of people here dressed as seats!” Vicky giggled nervously. The rest of the chat came and went perfectly amiably. Jezza did what he does best, giving his best impression of a multimillionaire held back by the incompetence of government. Still, at least he injected some fun. Vicky wanted to know how the farming summer had gone. He replied that the Diddly Squat farm had produced several ounces of hen food because of the extreme heat. Someone should have told him that Griffith was about to get rid of the Climate Change Committee. If you missed any of this, you will be able to watch extended highlights on the next series of Clarkson’s Farm. From then on, the conference became one long car crash. A panel with a couple of rightwing hacks droning on about nothing and then another panel in which one businesswoman congratulated herself on not getting stabbed on the train to Brum – apparently all her friends refuse to use trains – and then a businessman sobbing at the thought of billionaires being asked to pay inheritance tax. Some of them are so sick with worry they can no longer sleep. Finally the main attraction. What would turn out to be a landmark occasion for all party conferences. Because Griffith proceeded to give the worst speech ever heard. Not just in content but in delivery. It was like watching a less sentient version of the PG Tips monkey. Constantly applauding himself and ending his sentences with “Yeah”. What was left of the audience didn’t know where to look. If Andy really is the future chancellor, then we are truly fucked. Even Mel Stride wasn’t this hopeless. We might as well all pack up now. He was going to build more homes that were uninsulated and might fall down because they were cheaper. He would cut taxes and regulations the Tories had themselves introduced. “This is our destiny,” he said. And then he dematerialised. It was as though he had been primitive AI and his controller had seen quite enough and decommissioned him. Andy didn’t know he had finished. And neither did anyone else.
